questions.stem: A client with opioid use disorder who has not used opioids for several hours develops anxiety, sweating, yawning, dilated pupils, and abdominal cramping, and a new nurse assumes these symptoms actually point to an opioid overdose rather than the opposite. The nurse should recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An allergic reaction to a recently administered medication, since sweating and pupil changes can resemble hypersensitivity, rather than the actual process happening here","B":"Opioid withdrawal, which, while generally not life-threatening, causes significant distress and should be assessed and managed appropriately, rather than the overdose the new nurse assumed","C":"An expected physiological finding in this situation that would not typically require further nursing assessment, contrary to what this distressing presentation actually calls for","D":"A sign consistent with opioid overdose, similar to what the new nurse is currently assuming, since similar autonomic symptoms are thought to accompany excessive opioid effect"}}
questions.rationale: Anxiety, sweating, yawning, dilated pupils, and abdominal cramping are classic signs of opioid withdrawal, which typically begins several hours after the last use in a dependent individual. While generally not life-threatening (unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal), it causes significant distress and should be assessed using a validated tool and managed appropriately, which may include medication-assisted treatment.
questions.source_name: SAMHSA — Opioid Withdrawal Recognition and Management
questions.source_detail: Clinical Signs of Opioid Withdrawal

questions.stem: A hospitalized client who smokes regularly is unable to smoke during their stay and reports irritability, difficulty concentrating, increased appetite, and strong cravings. The nurse should recognize these as signs of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An allergic reaction to something recently eaten in the hospital, since these symptoms can resemble a hypersensitivity response","B":"Nicotine withdrawal, which the nurse can help address through strategies such as nicotine replacement therapy per provider order","C":"An expected, transient reaction unrelated to nicotine that would not typically require any nursing intervention","D":"A sign of an unrelated acute medical emergency requiring immediate escalation rather than routine nursing management"}}
questions.rationale: Irritability, difficulty concentrating, increased appetite, and cravings are common signs of nicotine withdrawal in a hospitalized smoker unable to use tobacco. The nurse can help address these symptoms and support the client's comfort through strategies such as nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum) per provider order, which can also serve as an opportunity to discuss smoking cessation resources.
questions.source_name: CDC — Nicotine Withdrawal and Hospital-Based Tobacco Cessation Support
questions.source_detail: Recognizing and Managing Nicotine Withdrawal in Hospitalized Clients

questions.stem: A nurse is distinguishing between malignant hyperthermia and heat stroke. The key distinguishing feature of malignant hyperthermia is that it:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Triggered by specific anesthetic agents such as succinylcholine or volatile agents in genetically susceptible people, typically during or shortly after surgery","B":"Has little established relationship to genetic predisposition or specific medication triggers at all, instead developing purely from external environmental heat exposure factors alone","C":"A chronic, slowly progressive condition that develops gradually over a span of many months or even years, rather than presenting suddenly as an acute emergency during surgery","D":"Occurs primarily due to external environmental heat exposure alone, developing through essentially the very same underlying physiologic mechanism as classic exertional heat stroke"}}
questions.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia is specifically triggered by certain anesthetic agents (such as succinylcholine or volatile inhaled anesthetics) in genetically susceptible individuals, typically occurring acutely during or shortly after surgical anesthesia — distinct from heat stroke, which results from environmental heat exposure and/or exertion, though both are hypermetabolic emergencies requiring rapid cooling and supportive treatment.
questions.source_name: MHAUS (Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States) — MH vs. Heat-Related Illness Distinction
questions.source_detail: Trigger and Context Differences Between MH and Heat Stroke

questions.stem: A post-operative client develops tachycardia, hypotension, and increased sanguineous drainage from the surgical site, and a colleague initially assumes this is likely just an allergic reaction to the anesthetic given some overlapping symptoms. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An expected post-operative finding that would not typically require further assessment or provider notification, contrary to the urgency this particular combination of findings suggests","B":"An allergic reaction to the anesthetic agent, since similar hemodynamic changes can accompany hypersensitivity reactions, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","C":"Bleeding at the surgical site severe enough to need urgent evaluation, notification of the provider, and prompt intervention","D":"A urinary tract infection, since fever and tachycardia are thought to commonly present with this type of infection, which does not fit this particular presentation"}}
questions.rationale: Tachycardia, hypotension, and increased sanguineous (bloody) drainage from a surgical site are classic signs of post-operative hemorrhage, a potentially serious complication requiring immediate further assessment (vital signs, wound/dressing inspection, possible lab work), prompt provider notification, and intervention to prevent hypovolemic shock.
questions.source_name: AORN — Postoperative Hemorrhage Recognition and Management
questions.source_detail: Clinical Signs of Post-Operative Hemorrhage

questions.stem: A nurse is identifying risk factors for pressure injury development in a hospitalized client. Which factor would place a client at increased risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Excellent nutritional status with adequate protein intake and no other identifiable pressure injury risk factors present","B":"Ability to independently reposition every couple of hours without requiring staff assistance or reminders","C":"Full mobility with an independent repositioning ability and no reported sensory or nutritional impairment","D":"Immobility, impaired sensory perception, poor nutrition, and excessive moisture (such as from incontinence)"}}
questions.rationale: Key risk factors for pressure injury development include immobility (inability to independently reposition), impaired sensory perception (reduced ability to feel and respond to pressure/discomfort), poor nutritional status, and excessive moisture (such as from incontinence), all of which are assessed as part of tools like the Braden Scale to guide individualized prevention strategies.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Pressure Injury Risk Factor Assessment
questions.source_detail: Key Risk Factors for Pressure Injury Development

questions.stem: A nurse uses the Caprini score to assess a surgical client's risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), and a student assumes a higher score would actually mean the client needs less aggressive prophylaxis since they must be doing well overall. A higher Caprini score instead indicates:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A lower overall VTE risk, since the scoring system is designed to identify clients who need less prophylaxis, similar to what the student is currently assuming","B":"A tool used specifically for assessing cardiac surgical risk before valve or bypass procedures, rather than venous thromboembolism risk, which does not describe what this score actually measures","C":"Higher VTE risk, which may warrant more intensive prophylaxis, such as pharmacologic measures added to mechanical ones","D":"A score with little established connection to VTE risk stratification, functioning mainly as a general post-operative recovery checklist"}}
questions.rationale: The Caprini score is a validated risk assessment tool that assigns points based on various VTE risk factors (such as age, surgery type, mobility, and medical history), with a higher total score indicating greater VTE risk, which may guide the decision for more intensive prophylactic measures, including pharmacologic prophylaxis in addition to mechanical methods.
questions.source_name: American College of Chest Physicians — VTE Risk Assessment and Prophylaxis Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Caprini Score and VTE Risk Stratification

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a client's ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification before surgery, and a family member assumes this number reflects the surgical team's own skill level rather than anything about the client. This classification is instead used to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Primarily measure the surgical team's technical skill and experience rather than the client's own health status, similar to what the family member is currently assuming","B":"Determine a client's insurance coverage for the planned surgical procedure, which is not the actual purpose of this particular classification","C":"Categorize a client's overall physical health and anesthesia-related risk before a surgical procedure, rather than the surgical team's skill as the family member assumed","D":"Assess a client's nutritional status rather than their overall surgical risk, which is not what this particular classification actually measures"}}
questions.rationale: The ASA physical status classification system categorizes a client's overall physical health status (ranging from ASA I, a healthy client, to ASA VI, a declared brain-dead client for organ donation) before a surgical procedure, helping assess anesthesia-related risk and inform perioperative planning.
questions.source_name: American Society of Anesthesiologists — ASA Physical Status Classification System
questions.source_detail: Purpose of ASA Classification in Preoperative Assessment

questions.stem: A nurse is selecting an appropriate pain assessment scale for a young child who cannot yet reliably use a numeric rating scale. An appropriate alternative is:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A scale requiring the child to rate pain on a 0-10 numeric scale, without regard for their own developmental ability","B":"No pain assessment tool being considered appropriate for use with young children","C":"Assuming the child has no pain, since verbal self-report happens to be unavailable","D":"A developmentally appropriate scale, such as the FACES pain scale, which uses facial expressions rather than numbers"}}
questions.rationale: For young children who cannot reliably use a numeric rating scale, a developmentally appropriate alternative such as the FACES pain scale (using a series of facial expressions ranging from happy/no pain to crying/worst pain) is recommended, allowing for more accurate, age-appropriate pain assessment.
questions.source_name: Wong-Baker FACES Foundation — Pediatric Pain Assessment Tools
questions.source_detail: Selecting Developmentally Appropriate Pain Scales

questions.stem: A nurse uses a validated malnutrition screening tool, such as the MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool), during a client's admission assessment, and a colleague assumes nutritional status will just naturally correct itself once the client starts eating hospital meals again. This screening is important because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Nutritional status is considered to have relatively limited bearing on wound healing or immune function, since it is assumed to correct itself during recovery, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","B":"This tool is understood to replace the need for any further, more detailed nutritional assessment once the initial screening is complete","C":"Early identification of malnutrition risk allows for timely nutritional intervention, improving wound healing, immune function, and overall outcomes","D":"This tool is considered relevant mainly for elective outpatient visits, since inpatient nutritional needs are assumed to be addressed automatically through hospital meal service"}}
questions.rationale: Early identification of malnutrition risk through validated screening tools allows for timely nutritional intervention (such as dietary supplementation or specialist referral), which can improve wound healing, immune function, and overall clinical outcomes, since malnutrition is associated with increased complications and longer hospital stays.
questions.source_name: BAPEN (British Association for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition) / ASPEN — Malnutrition Screening Importance
questions.source_detail: Value of Early Malnutrition Risk Identification

questions.stem: A nurse reviews preoperative laboratory testing ordered for a client before elective surgery, and a family member assumes every client gets the exact same standard panel regardless of their own health background. The purpose of this testing is generally instead to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Be applied in an identical, standardized fashion to every client, regardless of health status, age, or the type of surgical procedure planned, similar to what the family member is currently assuming","B":"Mainly add time to the surgical scheduling process, without providing information that meaningfully changes the anesthesia plan","C":"Serve as a substitute for a thorough history and physical exam, allowing the provider to rely on lab values alone for risk assessment","D":"Identify underlying conditions or abnormalities that could affect surgical or anesthesia risk, allowing for optimization or precautions beforehand"}}
questions.rationale: Preoperative laboratory testing (individualized based on the client's health status, planned procedure, and risk factors, rather than a blanket approach for all clients) is intended to identify any underlying conditions or abnormalities (such as anemia, electrolyte imbalances, or coagulation issues) that could affect surgical or anesthesia risk, allowing the care team to optimize the client's condition or take appropriate precautions before proceeding.
questions.source_name: American Society of Anesthesiologists — Preoperative Evaluation Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Individualized Preoperative Testing

questions.stem: A nurse uses a facility-provided safe patient handling algorithm to determine the appropriate method and equipment for repositioning a specific client, and a colleague assumes this tool is really only meant for bariatric clients since standard-weight clients pose little handling risk. This tool is instead intended to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Serve as a full substitute for the nurse's own clinical judgment during a repositioning task, removing the need for individual assessment, rather than working alongside clinical judgment as it actually does","B":"Have little measurable effect on staff or client injury rates, since most handling injuries are assumed to result from unavoidable factors","C":"Provide a structured, evidence-based framework guiding decisions about the safest handling method based on the client's mobility level and other factors","D":"Be designed specifically for bariatric clients only, since standard-weight clients are assumed by the colleague to pose minimal handling risk to staff"}}
questions.rationale: Safe patient handling algorithms provide a structured, evidence-based framework to guide decision-making about the safest method and equipment for a specific task (such as repositioning or transferring), based on factors like the client's weight-bearing ability, cognitive status, and cooperation level, helping reduce injury risk for both clients and staff.
questions.source_name: ANA — Safe Patient Handling and Mobility Algorithms
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Safe Patient Handling Decision Algorithms

questions.stem: A nurse is planning personal hygiene care for a hospitalized client. The nurse understands that bathing frequency should generally be:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Performed on a single fixed occasion during the entire hospital stay, regardless of how the client's skin condition changes over time","B":"Individualized based on the client's skin condition, personal preferences, cultural considerations, and clinical status, rather than a rigid one-size-fits-all schedule","C":"Determined mainly by what is most convenient for staff workflow on a given shift, with limited attention paid to the client's own preference","D":"Delivered identically to every client on the unit on a fixed schedule, without adjustment for individual skin condition or comfort needs"}}
questions.rationale: Personal hygiene care, including bathing frequency, should be individualized based on the client's skin condition, personal preferences, cultural considerations, and clinical status (such as risk for skin breakdown or presence of excessive perspiration/soiling), rather than following a rigid, identical schedule for every client.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Individualized Personal Hygiene Care
questions.source_detail: Factors Guiding Individualized Bathing Frequency

questions.stem: A nurse is helping a post-operative client progressively increase their ambulation distance each day. This gradual progression approach is important because it:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Allows the client's tolerance, strength, and endurance to be reassessed and built upon gradually, reducing the risk of overexertion or injury while promoting recovery","B":"Kept identical for every client regardless of their specific surgical procedure, baseline mobility, or pre-operative functional status","C":"Started at the client's maximum tolerable distance from the very first post-operative day, rather than building up gradually over time","D":"Considered to have relatively little bearing on how safely a client regains functional mobility, since recovery is assumed to progress at its own pace"}}
questions.rationale: Gradual, individualized progression of ambulation distance allows the nurse to reassess the client's tolerance, strength, and endurance at each step, building activity level safely over time, reducing the risk of overexertion, falls, or other complications, while still promoting the well-established benefits of early, progressive mobility after surgery.
questions.source_name: AORN — Progressive Postoperative Ambulation Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Benefits of Gradual Ambulation Progression

questions.stem: A nurse is providing end-of-life comfort care for a dying client. Priority comfort measures generally include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Limiting most forms of direct care and interaction, in the belief that this reduces unnecessary stimulation","B":"Setting aside the client's and family's expressed wishes in favor of the care team's own clinical priorities","C":"Continuing aggressive curative treatment measures despite the client's stated preference to focus on comfort","D":"Effective pain and symptom management, along with attention to psychological, spiritual, and family support needs"}}
questions.rationale: End-of-life comfort (palliative) care prioritizes effective pain and symptom management (such as addressing dyspnea, nausea, or anxiety), along with attention to the psychological, spiritual, and emotional needs of both the client and family, focusing on dignity and quality of remaining life rather than curative intervention, in alignment with the client's and family's wishes.
questions.source_name: National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization — End-of-Life Comfort Care Standards
questions.source_detail: Priorities in End-of-Life Comfort Care

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion counseling to a client experiencing significant work-related stress. Evidence-based stress management strategies the nurse might suggest include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular physical activity, relaxation techniques (such as deep breathing or mindfulness), adequate sleep, and seeking social support","B":"Assuming the work-related stress will resolve on its own once the current busy period ends, without needing any active coping strategy","C":"Limiting physical activity as much as possible during stressful periods, in order to conserve energy for other daily demands and responsibilities","D":"Increasing reliance on caffeine and alcohol as a primary strategy for managing day-to-day stress and improving sleep quality"}}
questions.rationale: Evidence-based stress management strategies include regular physical activity, relaxation techniques (such as deep breathing, mindfulness, or meditation), adequate sleep, maintaining social connections/support, and, when needed, professional support — all of which can help mitigate the negative health effects of chronic stress.
questions.source_name: CDC / NIOSH — Workplace Stress Management Resources
questions.source_detail: Evidence-Based Stress Management Strategies

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a breastfeeding client who is returning to work about maintaining milk supply. The nurse should advise the client that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular milk expression (pumping) at intervals similar to the infant's typical feeding schedule can help maintain milk supply while separated from the infant","B":"Considered largely incompatible with continuing to work outside the home, since most workplaces are assumed to lack adequate space or break time for pumping","C":"Expected to decline sharply and become difficult to sustain once regular daytime separation from the infant begins each week","D":"Limited by a general lack of workplace accommodations for breastfeeding employees, regardless of applicable federal break-time protections"}}
questions.rationale: Regular milk expression (pumping) at intervals similar to the infant's typical feeding schedule can help maintain milk supply while a breastfeeding mother is separated from her infant during work hours. Additionally, U.S. federal law (under the Fair Labor Standards Act, as amended) provides certain workplace protections and accommodations for breastfeeding employees to express milk.
questions.source_name: U.S. Department of Labor — Break Time for Nursing Mothers / CDC Breastfeeding and Return to Work Guidance
questions.source_detail: Maintaining Milk Supply and Workplace Accommodations

questions.stem: A nurse is providing SIDS (Sudden Infant Death Syndrome) risk reduction education to new parents. In addition to safe sleep positioning, the nurse should include which additional recommendation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Bringing the infant into the parents' bed for closer overnight monitoring during the earliest months of life","B":"Using thick blankets and extra pillows in the crib to help keep the infant warm throughout the night","C":"Avoiding smoke exposure, offering a pacifier at sleep time (once breastfeeding is established), and avoiding overheating the infant","D":"Continuing to smoke around the infant, since secondhand smoke exposure is not considered a meaningful SIDS risk factor"}}
questions.rationale: In addition to safe sleep positioning (back to sleep, firm surface), comprehensive SIDS risk reduction education includes avoiding infant exposure to smoke, offering a pacifier at sleep time (once breastfeeding is well-established, generally around 3-4 weeks), and avoiding overheating/overbundling the infant — all evidence-based recommendations from the AAP, while bed-sharing is not recommended.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — SIDS Risk Reduction Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Comprehensive Safe Sleep and SIDS Risk Reduction Guidance

questions.stem: A nurse is discussing psychological resilience with a client recovering from a significant life stressor. Protective factors associated with resilience generally include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Strong social support, effective coping skills, a sense of purpose or meaning, and adaptability","B":"A tendency toward rigid, inflexible thinking patterns that limit adaptation to new or changing circumstances","C":"Having experienced comparatively little adversity or stress over the course of one's life up to this point","D":"A pattern of social withdrawal and avoidance of support systems during periods of difficulty"}}
questions.rationale: Psychological resilience — the ability to adapt well in the face of adversity — is generally associated with protective factors including strong social support networks, effective coping skills, a sense of purpose or meaning, and cognitive/behavioral adaptability, rather than the complete absence of stress, which is not a realistic or necessary condition for resilience.
questions.source_name: APA (American Psychological Association) — Building Resilience Resource
questions.source_detail: Protective Factors Associated with Resilience

questions.stem: A client develops significant emotional distress and difficulty functioning within three months of a major life change, such as a job loss, with symptoms exceeding what would typically be expected for the stressor, but not meeting criteria for another specific mental health diagnosis, and a family member assumes this must be a longstanding personality issue rather than something tied to the recent job loss. The nurse should recognize this as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A stress-related reaction tied to the timing and nature of a specific triggering event, occurring within roughly three months of that event","B":"A condition understood to arise without any connection to an identifiable external stressor, developing instead independently of recent life events, contrary to the clear connection to this client's job loss","C":"An expected life transition that would not typically warrant clinical evaluation, since most people are assumed to adapt without noticeable distress","D":"A longstanding, pervasive personality disorder present since early adulthood, unrelated to any single recent stressor, similar to what the family member is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: Adjustment disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor, occurring within 3 months of the stressor's onset, with symptoms that are out of proportion to what would typically be expected, causing significant distress or functional impairment, but not meeting criteria for another specific mental health diagnosis.
questions.source_name: DSM-5-TR — Diagnostic Criteria for Adjustment Disorder
questions.source_detail: Core Features of Adjustment Disorder

questions.stem: A client presents with persistent, distressing physical symptoms and excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to these symptoms, such as high health-related anxiety or excessive time devoted to the symptoms, significantly impacting daily life, despite thorough medical evaluation, and a family member assumes the client must simply be faking these complaints for attention. The nurse should recognize this as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A pattern in which the client is understood to be deliberately fabricating or exaggerating symptoms for some clear external benefit, similar to what the family member is currently assuming","B":"A presentation considered entirely disconnected from any underlying psychological or emotional factor, arising instead from an as-yet-undiagnosed physical illness","C":"An expected, proportionate response to physical symptoms that essentially any person would be assumed to display in a comparable situation","D":"A condition where genuine bodily complaints come paired with outsized worry or life disruption that doesn't ease even after thorough medical reassurance"}}
questions.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder involves genuinely experienced, distressing physical symptoms accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to those symptoms (such as persistent high anxiety about health or excessive time and energy devoted to the symptoms), significantly impacting daily functioning — distinct from factitious disorder or malingering, since the symptoms and distress are not intentionally produced or fabricated.
questions.source_name: DSM-5-TR — Diagnostic Criteria for Somatic Symptom Disorder
questions.source_detail: Core Features of Somatic Symptom Disorder

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer NPH insulin, which appears cloudy/uniformly white after gentle mixing. The nurse should recognize that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An intermediate-acting suspension that should be gently rolled, not shaken","B":"Cloudy insulin should be warmed in hot water before use","C":"This cloudiness indicates contamination and the vial should be discarded","D":"The insulin should always appear clear, and cloudiness is abnormal"}}
questions.rationale: NPH insulin is a suspension (intermediate-acting) and is normally cloudy/uniformly white after gentle mixing, unlike clear rapid- or long-acting insulins. It should be gently rolled between the hands or inverted (not shaken vigorously, which can cause bubbling and inaccurate dosing) to evenly resuspend the particles before drawing up the dose.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — NPH Insulin
questions.source_detail: Proper Mixing Technique for Insulin Suspensions

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's beta-blocker prescription and notes it is metoprolol succinate rather than metoprolol tartrate, and a colleague assumes the two salt forms are basically identical with no real difference in how they're taken. The nurse should recognize that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"One formulation is extended-release taken once daily, the other immediate-release taken multiple times daily","B":"Metoprolol tartrate generally being the extended-release form, which reverses which formulation actually has that release profile","C":"The salt form having fairly little bearing on dosing frequency","D":"These are identical formulations with no clinical difference, similar to the colleague's current assumption about the two salt forms"}}
questions.rationale: Metoprolol succinate is an extended-release formulation typically dosed once daily (often used for conditions like heart failure and hypertension), while metoprolol tartrate is an immediate-release formulation typically dosed multiple times daily. These formulations are not interchangeable on a mg-for-mg basis without provider guidance, since substituting one for the other inappropriately can lead to dosing errors.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Metoprolol Succinate vs. Tartrate
questions.source_detail: Formulation Differences and Dosing Frequency

questions.stem: Before administering digoxin, the nurse should assess which vital sign, and hold the dose and notify the provider if it falls below a specific threshold?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg before administration","B":"Apical pulse, generally holding the dose if below 60 beats/min","C":"Temperature above 38 degrees Celsius before administration","D":"Respiratory rate below 12 breaths per minute before dosing"}}
questions.rationale: Before administering digoxin, the nurse should assess the apical pulse for a full minute, generally holding the dose and notifying the provider if the apical pulse is below 60 beats/min in an adult (parameters may be adjusted for pediatric clients or per specific facility policy), since digoxin can cause or worsen bradycardia.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Digoxin Administration Safety Check
questions.source_detail: Apical Pulse Assessment Before Digoxin Administration

questions.stem: A client is prescribed oral potassium chloride supplements. The nurse should instruct the client to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Take the medication on an empty stomach for best absorption","B":"Take with food or a full glass of water to reduce GI irritation","C":"Take the medication only once per week regardless of dose","D":"Chew extended-release tablets thoroughly before swallowing"}}
questions.rationale: Oral potassium chloride can cause significant GI irritation, including nausea, vomiting, and even ulceration in some cases. Taking the medication with food or a full glass of water helps reduce this irritation. Extended-release tablets/capsules should generally be swallowed whole, not chewed or crushed, unless specifically indicated otherwise.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Oral Potassium Chloride
questions.source_detail: Administration to Reduce GI Irritation

questions.stem: A nurse is administering IV phenytoin and notices swelling and a dark purple-blue discoloration developing around the IV site, with the client reporting pain, though there is no evidence of infiltration on ultrasound. The nurse should recognize this as a possible sign of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A simple bruise from insertion requiring no further action","B":"An indication to increase the infusion rate further","C":"'Purple glove syndrome,' requiring the infusion to be stopped","D":"A normal, expected finding requiring no further action"}}
questions.rationale: "Purple glove syndrome" is a rare but serious soft tissue injury associated with IV phenytoin administration, characterized by pain, edema, and purple-bluish discoloration at or distal to the injection site, sometimes occurring even without extravasation. Risk is reduced by administering phenytoin slowly (not exceeding facility/manufacturer-specified maximum rates) through a large-bore IV in a large vein. If suspected, the infusion should be stopped and the provider notified promptly.
questions.source_name: PMC — Purple Glove Syndrome: Recognizing a Rare Complication of IV Phenytoin
questions.source_detail: Recognition and Response to Purple Glove Syndrome

questions.stem: A client is prescribed isoniazid for latent tuberculosis infection, and mentions having noticed slightly darker urine over the past few days but assumes this is probably nothing worth mentioning. The nurse should teach the client to report which symptom, including what the client just described, that could indicate a serious adverse effect requiring prompt evaluation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Feeling a bit more tired than usual lately, with nothing else out of the ordinary noticed","B":"Jaundice, dark urine, or nausea/vomiting suggesting hepatotoxicity, directly relevant to the darker urine the client just described noticing","C":"Mild headache, without much other associated symptom, which would not capture the darker urine the client just mentioned","D":"A slight increase in appetite following the medication, which would not capture the concerning symptom the client just described"}}
questions.rationale: Isoniazid carries a risk of hepatotoxicity, which can range from mild transaminase elevation to severe, potentially fatal hepatitis. Clients should be taught to report symptoms such as jaundice, dark urine, unexplained nausea/vomiting, or abdominal pain promptly, since these may indicate liver injury requiring further evaluation and possible discontinuation of the medication.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Isoniazid
questions.source_detail: Warnings: Hepatotoxicity Signs to Report

questions.stem: A client newly prescribed rifampin for tuberculosis asks the nurse about a common, harmless side effect they may notice. The nurse should explain that rifampin commonly causes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Complete loss of taste sensation during treatment","B":"A harmless orange-red discoloration of body fluids and secretions","C":"No notable side effects of any kind whatsoever","D":"Permanent discoloration of the teeth over time"}}
questions.rationale: Rifampin commonly causes a harmless orange-red discoloration of body fluids, including urine, sweat, tears, and saliva. Clients should be informed of this expected effect in advance to prevent unnecessary alarm, and those who wear soft contact lenses should be cautioned that the lenses may become permanently stained.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Rifampin
questions.source_detail: Expected Body Fluid Discoloration

questions.stem: A nurse notes that a client with Clostridioides difficile colitis is prescribed oral vancomycin, while a client with a systemic MRSA bloodstream infection is prescribed IV vancomycin, and a student assumes this must be an error since it's the same drug. The nurse should understand that this route difference reflects:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Poor systemic absorption when taken orally, keeping it concentrated in the gut, while IV dosing reaches the systemic levels needed","B":"A route difference based solely on cost considerations, with little clinical basis behind choosing one route over the other for either client","C":"Fairly little meaningful difference between the two routes, contrary to why these two clients were prescribed different administration methods","D":"A prescribing error, since vancomycin should generally be given IV, similar to what the student is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: Oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed systemically, remaining largely within the GI tract, making it ideal for treating C. difficile colitis, a local GI infection. In contrast, IV vancomycin is required to achieve adequate systemic drug levels needed to treat a systemic infection, such as a MRSA bloodstream infection, since oral vancomycin would not reach therapeutic levels outside the gut.
questions.source_name: IDSA — Clostridioides difficile Infection Treatment Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Rationale for Oral vs. IV Vancomycin Route Selection

questions.stem: A nurse is flushing a heparin lock to maintain patency and encounters some resistance partway through, though a colleague suggests just pushing a bit harder to clear whatever is blocking it. The nurse should instead use which technique?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Flushing with tap water instead of a sterile solution, in order to more effectively clear whatever might be causing this resistance","B":"A push-pause technique, stopping if resistance is ever met, rather than pushing harder as the colleague is currently suggesting","C":"Forceful, rapid flushing without much regard for the resistance felt, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting doing","D":"Fairly little flushing being needed for this particular device, contrary to why the nurse is performing this task in the first place"}}
questions.rationale: Proper technique for flushing an intermittent IV access device (heparin/saline lock) includes using a "push-pause" method with an appropriate sterile flush solution (per facility protocol, which may include normal saline alone or with heparin), and stopping immediately if resistance is met — never forcing a flush against resistance, since this could dislodge a clot or cause other complications.
questions.source_name: Infusion Nurses Society — IV Flushing and Locking Standards
questions.source_detail: Proper Flushing Technique for IV Access Devices

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a new prescription for a stimulant medication for ADHD for a client whose chart also notes a history of a mild arrhythmia, and the prescribing provider seems unaware of this cardiac history. The nurse should be aware that stimulant medications carry a warning regarding:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A guaranteed improvement in cardiac function with use, which would actually understate the risk this client's cardiac history poses here","B":"No cardiovascular risk of any kind with this medication class, contrary to why this client's cardiac history is actually relevant to flag","C":"A risk limited only to respiratory effects rather than cardiac ones, which does not accurately describe this medication class's actual warning","D":"Increased heart rate and blood pressure, warranting cardiac caution, especially given this client's arrhythmia history"}}
questions.rationale: Stimulant medications used for conditions like ADHD can increase heart rate and blood pressure, and FDA labeling includes warnings regarding cardiovascular risk, generally recommending caution or avoidance in clients with serious underlying structural cardiac abnormalities or other serious heart conditions, given the risk of sudden cardiac events in this population.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Stimulant Medications
questions.source_detail: Cardiovascular Risk Warnings

questions.stem: A nurse anticipates a procedure with potential splash or spray risk of blood or body fluids. Standard precautions require the nurse to wear:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only a surgical mask, with no eye protection needed","B":"Eye protection, along with other PPE, to shield the mucous membranes","C":"No additional protection needed beyond gloves alone","D":"Eye protection only if specifically requested by the client"}}
questions.rationale: Standard precautions require eye protection (goggles or a face shield) whenever a procedure or activity carries a reasonably anticipated risk of blood or body fluid splash or spray to the face, protecting the mucous membranes of the eyes from potential pathogen exposure, in addition to other appropriate PPE such as gloves and a mask/gown as indicated.
questions.source_name: CDC — Standard Precautions, Eye Protection Requirements
questions.source_detail: When Eye Protection Is Required Under Standard Precautions

questions.stem: Between two surgical cases in the same operating room, environmental services staff perform cleaning and disinfection. This practice is important to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Applying only after cases involving known infections","B":"Replacing the need for sterile technique in the next case","C":"Reducing surgical site infection by removing surface pathogens","D":"Saving time, with no infection prevention purpose at all"}}
questions.rationale: Cleaning and disinfection of the operating room environment between surgical cases is an important infection prevention practice that helps reduce the risk of surgical site infection by removing potential pathogens from environmental surfaces, performed after every case (not just those involving known infections), in addition to (not as a replacement for) sterile technique during the procedure itself.
questions.source_name: AORN — Environmental Cleaning Guideline for the Operating Room
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Between-Case OR Cleaning

questions.stem: A nurse is using an alcohol-based hand sanitizer for hand hygiene. Correct technique includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Using the sanitizer for only 2-3 seconds regardless of coverage","B":"Applying sanitizer over visibly soiled hands without washing first","C":"Applying a small amount and wiping hands dry immediately","D":"Covering all surfaces and rubbing until completely dry"}}
questions.rationale: Correct alcohol-based hand sanitizer technique involves applying enough product to cover all surfaces of the hands and rubbing them together until completely dry (generally taking about 20 seconds), without rinsing or wiping with a towel, which would remove the antimicrobial effect. Visibly soiled hands should be washed with soap and water rather than relying on alcohol-based sanitizer alone.
questions.source_name: WHO / CDC — Hand Hygiene Technique for Alcohol-Based Hand Rub
questions.source_detail: Proper Application and Duration of Alcohol-Based Sanitizer

questions.stem: A nurse is exiting a room where a client is on airborne precautions, and the room has an anteroom, a small transitional space, though a new colleague heads straight for the nurses' station still wearing full PPE. The nurse should instead remove most PPE:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Believing the specific location of PPE removal has no bearing on infection control, similar to what the new colleague's actions suggest","B":"Only after fully returning to the nurses' station, similar to what the new colleague appears to be doing by leaving PPE on","C":"In the anteroom, with the respirator often removed last, rather than carrying PPE all the way to the nurses' station as the colleague is doing","D":"While still inside the client's room, before exiting into the anteroom at all"}}
questions.rationale: When an anteroom is available (a small transitional space between the client's room and the hallway), most PPE is generally removed in the anteroom before exiting into the general hallway, per facility protocol, helping contain potential contamination — with the respirator (such as an N95) often removed last, sometimes just after leaving the room itself, following specific facility sequencing.
questions.source_name: CDC — PPE Doffing Sequence for Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms
questions.source_detail: Location for PPE Removal When an Anteroom Is Present

questions.stem: A client is placed on droplet precautions. The nurse should ensure that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Signage placed only inside the room, not at the entrance","B":"Signage only needed for airborne, not droplet, precautions","C":"No signage needed, since staff should already know the type","D":"Clear signage posted at the entrance before any entry"}}
questions.rationale: Clear signage indicating the specific type of isolation precautions in place and the required PPE should be posted at the room entrance (visible before entry), ensuring all staff, visitors, and ancillary personnel are informed and can don appropriate PPE before entering, regardless of the specific precaution type (contact, droplet, or airborne).
questions.source_name: CDC — Isolation Precautions Signage Guidance
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Placement of Isolation Signage

questions.stem: A nurse is providing care for a single client that involves wound care followed immediately by handling clean linens for the same client, and a colleague suggests there's no need to change gloves since it's still the same person being cared for. The nurse should instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid gloves largely since just one client is involved in both of these tasks, similar to what the colleague seems to be suggesting","B":"Change gloves and perform hand hygiene between these two tasks, rather than keeping the same gloves on as the colleague suggested","C":"Wear the same gloves throughout both tasks for this one client, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting","D":"Just change gloves when moving to a different client entirely, rather than between different tasks for the same client as is actually needed here"}}
questions.rationale: Gloves should be changed, with hand hygiene performed, between different tasks or procedures on the same client (such as after wound care and before handling clean linens or a different body site), to prevent cross-contamination between contaminated and clean areas or tasks, not just when moving between different clients.
questions.source_name: CDC — Standard Precautions, Glove Use Between Tasks
questions.source_detail: Changing Gloves Between Tasks for the Same Client

questions.stem: A nurse is disposing of various types of waste generated during client care, including a used needle, a blood-soaked dressing, and a leftover unused vial of medication, and a colleague suggests just tossing everything into the same regular trash bin to save time. Proper waste segregation instead requires distinguishing between:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular, biohazardous, sharps, and pharmaceutical waste, each handled distinctly, rather than combined into one bin as the colleague suggested","B":"Just sharps waste requiring special handling, with everything else, including the dressing and medication vial, going into regular trash as the colleague suggested","C":"Essentially all waste being treated identically with fairly little categorization needed, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting","D":"Waste segregation having little relevance to safety or compliance, contrary to why these categories actually exist and matter here"}}
questions.rationale: Proper medical waste management requires segregating different waste categories — regular (non-hazardous) waste, regulated medical/biohazardous waste, sharps waste, and pharmaceutical/hazardous drug waste — each requiring distinct, appropriate disposal methods per facility protocol and regulatory requirements, to ensure safety and proper handling throughout the waste stream.
questions.source_name: EPA / OSHA — Medical Waste Management and Segregation Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Categories of Medical Waste Requiring Distinct Disposal

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains the difference between disinfection and sterilization to new staff, one of whom assumes the two terms are basically interchangeable ways of saying "very clean." The key distinction is instead that sterilization:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Is identical to disinfection with no meaningful difference, similar to what the new staff member is currently assuming","B":"Applies only to surfaces, never to instruments, which does not accurately describe what sterilization actually covers","C":"Is a less thorough process than disinfection overall, which reverses the actual relationship between these two terms","D":"Destroying all microbial life, including bacterial spores, unlike disinfection"}}
questions.rationale: Sterilization destroys all forms of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores, representing the highest level of microbial elimination — used for items requiring the highest level of safety (such as surgical instruments). Disinfection eliminates most pathogenic microorganisms but does not reliably destroy all bacterial spores, making it appropriate for a different category of items/surfaces based on their intended use and infection risk (per the Spaulding classification).
questions.source_name: CDC — Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities
questions.source_detail: Distinguishing Sterilization from Disinfection

questions.stem: A hospital tracks specific quality indicators, such as fall rates and pressure injury incidence, that are considered directly influenced by nursing care, and a physician colleague assumes these numbers mainly reflect medical rather than nursing decisions. These are instead known as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Physician-sensitive indicators, unrelated to nursing, similar to what the physician colleague is currently assuming about these particular metrics","B":"Nurse-sensitive indicators reflecting nursing care quality, rather than the physician-driven metrics the colleague assumed these to be","C":"Indicators with no established measurement framework, contrary to how these specific quality metrics are actually tracked and used","D":"Metrics used exclusively for billing purposes, with little clinical relevance, contrary to why these are actually tracked here"}}
questions.rationale: Nurse-sensitive quality indicators (such as fall rates, pressure injury incidence, and hospital-acquired infection rates) are outcome measures considered to be directly influenced by the quantity or quality of nursing care, used to evaluate and improve nursing practice and patient safety.
questions.source_name: ANA — Nurse-Sensitive Quality Indicators Framework
questions.source_detail: Definition and Purpose of Nurse-Sensitive Indicators

questions.stem: A hospital participates in the National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI) to benchmark its nurse-sensitive outcomes against other facilities, and a new manager assumes this data mainly just sits in a report with no real follow-up. The purpose of this participation is instead to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Replace the need for any internal quality improvement, similar to what the new manager's assumption about this data suggests","B":"Compare unit data against national benchmarks to guide improvement efforts, rather than simply sit unused as the new manager is currently assuming","C":"Have no impact on quality improvement efforts at all, similar to what the new manager is currently assuming about this data","D":"Focus solely on financial metrics with no clinical relevance, contrary to what this particular database actually tracks and is used for"}}
questions.rationale: Participation in a national nursing quality database such as NDNQI allows hospitals to compare their unit-level nurse-sensitive outcome data against national benchmarks, helping identify specific areas for improvement, track progress over time, and support evidence-based nursing quality initiatives.
questions.source_name: Press Ganey / ANA — NDNQI Purpose and Benchmarking Value
questions.source_detail: Value of National Nursing Quality Benchmarking

questions.stem: A nurse makes an independent clinical decision within their scope of practice and is prepared to answer for the outcomes of that decision. This reflects the professional nursing concept of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Professional accountability, accepting responsibility for decisions","B":"Delegation exclusively, with no personal responsibility","C":"A concept with no relevance to professional standards","D":"Avoidance of independent clinical judgment entirely"}}
questions.rationale: Professional accountability refers to a nurse's acceptance of responsibility for their own actions, clinical decisions, and the outcomes of those decisions, a foundational concept in professional nursing practice reflected in codes of ethics, scope of practice standards, and licensure requirements.
questions.source_name: ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses — Professional Accountability
questions.source_detail: Core Concept of Nursing Accountability

questions.stem: A nurse licensed in a non-compact state wants to provide telehealth nursing services to a client located in a different state, and assumes that since the visit is virtual, no additional state licensing considerations would apply. The nurse should instead understand that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Telehealth is exempt from all state licensure laws, similar to what the nurse is currently assuming about this kind of virtual visit","B":"Their home state license permits practice everywhere automatically, similar to the nurse's current assumption about telehealth","C":"No licensure considerations apply across state lines for this kind of virtual encounter, similar to what the nurse is currently assuming","D":"They generally need licensure in the state where the client is located, contrary to the nurse's assumption that the virtual format removes this requirement"}}
questions.rationale: Absent specific compact or reciprocity arrangements, telehealth nursing practice is generally governed by the location of the client (patient) receiving care, meaning the nurse typically needs to hold licensure or otherwise meet the legal requirements of the state where the client is physically located at the time of the encounter — an important consideration given the interstate nature of telehealth.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — Telehealth Nursing Practice and Interstate Licensure Considerations
questions.source_detail: Licensure Requirements for Interstate Telehealth Practice

questions.stem: A nurse manager encourages staff to review current nursing research literature when developing new unit protocols. This practice reflects the value of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A practice relevant only to academic nursing settings","B":"Nursing research having no practical application to bedside care","C":"Relying solely on tradition, with no role for research","D":"Incorporating evidence-based practice into protocol development"}}
questions.rationale: Incorporating current nursing research findings into clinical decision-making and protocol development reflects the value of evidence-based practice, helping ensure that nursing care and unit protocols are grounded in the most current, effective, and safe standards of care, rather than relying solely on tradition or personal experience.
questions.source_name: Sigma Theta Tau International / AACN — Evidence-Based Practice in Nursing
questions.source_detail: Value of Nursing Research in Clinical Practice

questions.stem: A hospital unit tracks its monthly fall rate and pressure injury incidence as part of ongoing quality monitoring. This data is used to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Replacing the need for individualized client risk assessment","B":"Having no practical application beyond record-keeping","C":"Identifying trends and guiding targeted improvement efforts","D":"Punishing individual staff members for any occurrence"}}
questions.rationale: Ongoing tracking of nurse-sensitive quality indicators such as fall rate and pressure injury incidence helps identify trends over time, evaluate the effectiveness of prevention interventions already in place, and guide targeted quality improvement efforts — a proactive, systems-level approach rather than a tool for individual staff punishment.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Quality Indicator Tracking for Continuous Improvement
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Ongoing Fall and Pressure Injury Data Tracking

questions.stem: A nurse is discussing nurse staffing legislation with colleagues from other states, and one colleague assumes every state must have essentially the same mandated staffing ratio laws by now. The nurse should instead understand that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Staffing legislation actually varies by state, ranging from mandated ratios to no legislation at all, contrary to the colleague's assumption of uniform laws","B":"No state having any staffing-related legislation at all, contrary to what actually exists across a number of states today","C":"All states having identical mandated staffing ratio laws in place, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","D":"Staffing legislation being determined solely at the federal level, contrary to how this issue is actually regulated across different states"}}
questions.rationale: States vary significantly in their regulatory approach to nurse staffing — some states (such as California) have legally mandated minimum nurse-to-patient ratios, while others require hospital staffing committees with nurse input, public reporting of staffing levels, or have no specific staffing legislation at all, reflecting an evolving and geographically varied policy landscape.
questions.source_name: ANA — State Nurse Staffing Legislation Overview
questions.source_detail: Variation in State Approaches to Staffing Regulation

questions.stem: A nurse is repeatedly asked by a supervisor to perform tasks that fall outside the legally defined scope of nursing practice in their state, and the supervisor insists that as the boss, their instructions simply override any other consideration. The nurse's appropriate response instead includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assuming supervisor instructions generally override the law, similar to what the supervisor is currently insisting in this situation","B":"Declining the task and escalating through appropriate channels, rather than simply deferring to the supervisor's instructions as insisted","C":"Complying without question to largely avoid conflict, similar to what the supervisor's insistence is currently pressuring the nurse to do","D":"Performing the task whenever no one else happens to be around, without much regard for the scope-of-practice concern the supervisor is asking the nurse to set aside"}}
questions.rationale: A nurse has a professional and legal responsibility to decline tasks that fall outside their legally defined scope of practice, regardless of supervisor pressure, since practicing outside one's legal scope exposes both the client and the nurse to significant risk. If pressure continues, the nurse should escalate the concern through appropriate channels (such as risk management or nursing leadership).
questions.source_name: NCSBN — Scope of Practice Decision-Making and Unauthorized Practice
questions.source_detail: Nursing Responsibility to Decline Out-of-Scope Tasks

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client in the early stages of shock whose blood pressure reading looks reassuringly normal, though the heart rate is notably elevated, and a colleague assumes the normal blood pressure rules out shock entirely. The nurse understands that in compensatory (early) shock, the body's compensatory mechanisms are instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Still maintaining near-normal blood pressure via tachycardia, meaning the normal-looking reading the colleague noticed doesn't actually rule out early shock","B":"Resulting in bradycardia as the primary early finding, which does not match this client's actual elevated heart rate","C":"Having no effect on vital signs at this early stage, contrary to the compensatory tachycardia actually occurring in this client","D":"Having already failed completely, with severe hypotension present, which does not match this client's still-normal blood pressure reading"}}
questions.rationale: In the compensatory (early) stage of shock, the body's compensatory mechanisms (such as tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction) are still able to maintain a relatively normal blood pressure, though subtle signs of hypoperfusion (such as mild tachycardia, anxiety, or slightly delayed capillary refill) may be present, requiring vigilant assessment to detect shock before progression to the decompensated stage, where hypotension becomes evident.
questions.source_name: Society of Critical Care Medicine — Stages of Shock
questions.source_detail: Compensatory vs. Decompensated Shock Distinction

questions.stem: A nurse is classifying a client's burn injury. A burn involving the epidermis and part of the dermis, presenting with blistering, redness, and significant pain, would be classified as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Full-thickness (third-degree) burn affecting all layers","B":"Partial-thickness burn with blistering and significant pain","C":"A burn with no clinical classification system available","D":"Superficial (first-degree) burn affecting only the epidermis"}}
questions.rationale: A partial-thickness (second-degree) burn involves the epidermis and part of the dermis, characteristically presenting with blistering, redness, and significant pain (since nerve endings remain intact), distinct from superficial (first-degree) burns (epidermis only, no blistering) and full-thickness (third-degree) burns (through the full dermis, often with reduced pain due to nerve destruction).
questions.source_name: American Burn Association — Burn Depth Classification
questions.source_detail: Classification of Partial-Thickness (Second-Degree) Burns

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client with frostbite of the fingers, noting the skin appears white/pale and feels hard and frozen to the touch, but only the outer skin layers appear affected with no blistering yet visible, and a family member assumes this must already be severe enough to require amputation. This would instead be classified as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A stage requiring immediate amputation of the affected digit, contrary to what this earlier-stage presentation actually calls for","B":"A milder cold injury limited to the top skin layer, not yet deep enough to cause blisters","C":"A condition entirely unrelated to cold exposure, contrary to the clear cold-exposure history behind this presentation","D":"A normal, unremarkable finding requiring no further care, contrary to the follow-up this frostbite still actually requires"}}
questions.rationale: Superficial (first-degree) frostbite typically presents with white/pale, hard, frozen-feeling skin affecting only the outer skin layers, without blistering. As frostbite progresses to deeper degrees, findings can include blistering (second-degree) and involvement of deeper tissues, including muscle and bone (more severe degrees), with worse prognosis for tissue viability.
questions.source_name: Wilderness Medical Society — Frostbite Classification and Staging
questions.source_detail: Classification of Superficial (First-Degree) Frostbite

questions.stem: A nurse is differentiating between syncope and near-syncope for a client who reports a brief episode of lightheadedness but insists they never actually lost consciousness. The nurse understands that syncope specifically involves:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A permanent loss of consciousness lasting indefinitely, which overstates what syncope actually describes as a clinical event","B":"A transient, complete loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery, distinguishing it from the near-syncope this particular client is actually describing","C":"A condition entirely unrelated to blood flow to the brain, contrary to the actual mechanism behind this presentation","D":"A brief lightheaded feeling with no loss of consciousness, which actually describes this client's near-syncope rather than true syncope"}}
questions.rationale: Syncope is defined as a transient, complete loss of consciousness and postural tone due to temporarily reduced cerebral blood flow, typically with rapid, spontaneous, and complete recovery — distinct from near-syncope (presyncope), which involves the sensation of impending loss of consciousness (lightheadedness, graying vision) without an actual complete loss of consciousness.
questions.source_name: American College of Cardiology / AHA — Syncope Evaluation Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Definition and Distinction of Syncope vs. Near-Syncope
